conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping those, but we lowered the ruxolitinib dose temporarily because of the infection. We don’t want to over-suppress your immune system while you’re fighting this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to do a bronchoscopy to get a sample from your lungs. It might help us find the exact cause of the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s routine. We’ll use a scope through your nose or mouth to look into your airways and take a small biopsy. It’s the best way to get answers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went okay, but we found a complication. You developed a pneumothorax — a small collapsed lung — after the biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but we caught it early. We’ve placed a small chest tube to help your lung re-expand. You’ll need to stay in the ICU for a few hours for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray shows the lung is re-expanding. The pneumothorax is improving. We’ll keep the tube in for now and check again tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Did they find anything in the biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. The initial cultures didn’t grow anything, and the stains were negative for bacteria, fungi, and Pneumocystis. That’s actually good — it means it’s likely not a severe infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep the chest tube a little longer. The pneumothorax is small but persistent. We’ll try clamping it later today to see if it stays closed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Most of these resolve with the tube. We’ll remove it once we’re sure the lung stays inflated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — we clamped the tube and no air leaked. That means your lung is healing. We’ll remove the tube soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the pneumonia? Am I getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your breathing is improving, and the antibiotics are likely helping. Even though we didn’t find a specific bug, we’re treating it as a healthcare-associated pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram yesterday. It showed your heart function is lower than before — ejection fraction is about 35%.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heart failure? From the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It could be from the total body irradiation or other treatments. We’ve started a low-dose beta-blocker, metoprolol, to help protect your heart. Cardiology will see you as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’re holding off on other heart meds until we see how you do. The main thing is to avoid fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today shows no pneumothorax. The tube is out, and your lung looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe easier already. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on antibiotics for a full 8-day course. Your wound cultures showed mixed flora and gram-negative rods, so we’re continuing ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My leg ulcers again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but they’re not the main issue now. The wound team will keep managing them. We may discuss debridement options later — like special dressings or even maggot therapy if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is much better. Oxygen levels are normal on room air. We’re going to switch you from IV to oral antibiotics tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by the weekend. We want to make sure the infection is fully treated and your heart is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest chest X-ray shows no pneumonia progression. The old opacity is stable. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my GVHD meds? I was on prednisone 25 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping prednisone at 15 mg now. It was lowered during the infection. We’ll continue ruxolitinib at 5 mg twice daily — that’s helping your skin GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And sirolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reduced it to 0.5 mg daily. Your level was high, and it interacts with posaconazole. We’ll check it again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning discharge for tomorrow if all goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, especially the antibiotics and antifungals. Use Dakin’s solution for wound care as instructed. Watch for fever, increased shortness of breath, or wound redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments: with Dr. Patel in a week for oncology, pulmonary in two weeks for PFTs, and cardiology soon. We’ll send all the records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last chest X-ray today — it’s stable. No signs of pneumonia or pneumothorax. You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. This stay was rough, but I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just take it easy at home. Rest, stay hydrated, and keep up with your wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. We’ve reviewed everything — labs, imaging, your progress. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One thing — your posaconazole dose is increased to 200 mg daily. We found your level was low, so this will help prevent fungal infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 25 mg daily. It’s to protect your heart. Call if you feel dizzy or very tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — should I still get IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every month. But we recommend taking Lasix before the infusion to avoid fluid overload, since your heart function is reduced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll mention that to my team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. All set. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in today from clinic because of worsening shortness of breath and back pain. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. The shortness of breath has been getting worse over the past week, and really bad the last two days. It’s especially hard when I bend over or walk. I also have this deep back pain, mostly in my lower spine and on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned it feels harder to take a deep breath. Any cough, fever, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or cough. No chest pain either. But I do feel like my right leg is a bit weaker, and walking makes the back pain worse. I’ve been using my cane more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for that. We’ll check your strength and sensation. Given your history of GVHD and transplant, we need to be careful about infections and other complications. We’ve ordered a CT of your chest and spine to get more information.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had a lot of CTs before. Is this about my lungs again? Last time it was pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Your breathing issues could be related to your GVHD affecting the lungs or chest wall. But we also want to rule out infection or other causes. The back pain needs imaging too—we’re concerned about possible compression fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, like from the steroids? I’ve been on them a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Long-term steroid use can weaken bones. We’ll look at that. For now, we’re starting you on your usual antibiotics—ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin—since you’re prone to skin infections, and we don’t want those spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scans are back. The chest CT shows no clear pneumonia, but there’s a small 6 mm spot in your right upper lobe—ground-glass opacity. It’s not definite, could be early infection or just scarring from GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not pneumonia? But my breathing is worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Your pulmonary function tests from before show severe restrictive lung disease—FEV1 and FVC down to 18% predicted. That’s worse than last time. We think your shortness of breath is mostly from worsening chest wall stiffness due to scleroderma from GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s the scarring, not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly, yes. We also tested for viruses—respiratory panel was negative. No flu, RSV, or others. So we’re not treating for infection unless things change. Instead, we’re starting a steroid burst—IV methylprednisolone 125 mg daily—to try to slow the scarring process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More steroids? I’m already on prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re increasing it temporarily. We’re also stopping ruxolitinib. Even though it’s used for GVHD, your chest scarring has progressed on it, so we don’t think it’s helping anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The spine CT shows mild chronic compression fractures at L2 and L5, with overall low bone density. Likely from long-term steroids and inactivity. We’re keeping your oxycodone the same for now, but we’ll increase the breakthrough dose to 30 mg if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a brace or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. These aren’t new or unstable fractures. But we’re arranging a Reclast infusion—zoledronic acid—after discharge to help strengthen your bones. You’ll get that at clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also looked at your leg wound. The culture showed Pseudomonas, but it’s resistant to ciprofloxacin. Still, we’re keeping you on it because it’s covering other bacteria, and we don’t want to disrupt your current regimen unless necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been oozing blood and hurts a lot. The maggot therapy was too painful, so we stopped it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve added a topical metronidazole gel to help with inflammation and bacterial load. The wound team is changing dressings daily. We also sent photos to your dermatology team for review.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your echocardiogram yesterday showed a drop in heart function—ejection fraction is now 35%. We’ve started you on metoprolol to help protect your heart. Cardiology reviewed it and thinks it’s related to prior treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart? I haven’t had symptoms. Is this serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we need to monitor. It’s called systolic heart failure. The good news is your cardiac MRI showed no constriction, just mild dysfunction. We’ll keep you on metoprolol and plan to add an ACE inhibitor later if it doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my thyroid? My TSH was low on admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your TSH is suppressed at 0.06, but your free T4 is normal. This is likely non-thyroidal illness—common in hospitalized patients with chronic disease. We’ll keep your levothyroxine the same and recheck after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your vitamin D. It’s low—37 ng/mL. We gave you a 50,000-unit dose today. You’ll need that weekly for a few weeks, then switch to 800 units daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been deficient before. Is this related to my gut or skin issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely both. Malabsorption and limited sun exposure due to skin GVHD. Supplementing will help your bones and immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your breathing hasn’t worsened, and you’re off IV steroids now. We’re switching to oral prednisone—20 mg daily. That’s a bit higher than before, but we’ll taper it slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make my bones worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re balancing risks. The short-term benefit of reducing lung and skin scarring outweighs the bone risk, especially since we’re treating the bone loss with Reclast and vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your oncologist, dermatologist, and rheumatologist. They’ll manage your GVHD. Cardiology wants you in two weeks to check your heart. And wound care will continue dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we’re giving you an IV immunoglobulin infusion today. Your hypogammaglobulinemia puts you at risk for infections, and this will help boost your immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually get that every three weeks. Was I due?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we didn’t want to miss it. It’s part of your preventive care, especially with all the skin wounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable, and you’re breathing better. We’re planning to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds, especially the new prednisone dose and the weekly vitamin D. Use the metronidazole gel on your legs daily. Watch for fever, increased pain, or redness spreading from the wounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 30 mg every four hours as needed. Don’t hesitate to take it—your pain control is important. And keep using your cane to avoid falls.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send the discharge summary to your doctors. If you feel worse—shortness of breath, chest pain, or confusion—go to the ER or call your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up with everyone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your AML remains in remission. No signs of relapse. We’ll keep you on your antiviral and antifungal meds to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I worry about that every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But your blood counts are stable, and we’ve seen no blasts. You’re doing well managing a very complex set of conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for you. The nurse will go over your prescriptions and wound care. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You came in today with a fever and some right upper quadrant pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I started feeling weak last night, and I had this dull ache in my upper right side. I also felt nauseous. This morning I took my temperature and it was 100.7. I’ve been having more drainage from my leg wounds too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for that. We’ve started you on fluids and antibiotics—Vancomycin and Cefepime—for now, just to cover any possible infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your chest X-ray didn’t show pneumonia, and your blood pressure and oxygen are stable. But given your history of skin infections, especially with Pseudomonas, we’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ve had that before. But I’m on Cipro and Amoxicillin at home. Why aren’t we using those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We paused your home antibiotics because we’re using broader IV ones for now. We’ll reassess in a few days. We also sent blood and urine cultures to see if we can find the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain in my side—is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. It could be gallbladder-related. We’re going to do an ultrasound to check that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, thanks. I just want to make sure we’re not missing something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re watching everything closely. Your heart rate is a bit high, but that could be from the fever or pain. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your abdominal ultrasound showed gallbladder sludge, but no signs of infection or inflammation—so no cholecystitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s not the cause of the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The sludge itself isn’t dangerous, but it can sometimes cause discomfort. We think your symptoms are more likely from your skin wounds, which have been problematic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had Pseudomonas there before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re continuing Cefepime because it covers Pseudomonas. We stopped Vancomycin since your blood cultures are negative after 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about my other meds? I’m on a lot of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your Sirolimus and prednisone for GVHD. Your oncologist will talk to you about possibly restarting ruxolitinib after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound culture came back. It grew Pseudomonas again, but it’s resistant to Ciprofloxacin and Ceftazidime—so we’re glad we’re on Cefepime, which it’s sensitive to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Cefepime should be effective. We’ll continue it for now and switch back to your oral antibiotics before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I remember last time my ejection fraction dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cardiac MRI showed mild systolic dysfunction, but no constriction. We’re keeping you on metoprolol for now. No need to add more heart meds at this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your thyroid. Your TSH was low, and your free T4 was low too. So we’ve increased your levothyroxine from 88 to 100 mcg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling more tired than usual. Could that be why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very possibly. Low thyroid can cause fatigue. We’ll see if you feel better on the higher dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my mood—I’ve been feeling down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatry team saw you and recommended increasing your venlafaxine to 75 mg in the morning and 37.5 mg at night. They think it might help with your energy and mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I just want to feel more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Your white count is stable, and liver enzymes are coming down. You’ve stayed afebrile since admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. We want to make sure your pain is well managed and your wounds are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My back’s been hurting more. I know I have compression fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from your last CT. The pain team saw you and recommended reducing your OxyContin from 30 to 20 mg twice daily and increasing gabapentin to 900 mg three times a day to help with nerve pain and reduce opioid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay with that. I don’t want to rely too much on opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound care team says your ulcers are looking better—less redness and drainage. We’ll keep the dressings going and send you home with supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried they weren’t healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re improving. We’ll restart your Cipro and Amoxicillin before discharge to prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s plan is to prepare for discharge tomorrow. We’ll finalize your meds and give you instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your temperature daily. If you spike a fever again, or if your wounds start oozing more, call your doctor. Also, weigh yourself every morning—let us know if you gain more than three pounds, which could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my new meds—ruxolitinib—I start that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oncologist wants you to start 5 mg twice daily when you get home, as part of a study. Make sure to follow up with them soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I appreciate all the coordination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your labs are stable, you’re afebrile, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What’s the final med list?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your Sirolimus, prednisone, and adding back Cipro and Amoxicillin. OxyContin is now 20 mg twice daily, gabapentin 900 mg three times a day, and levothyroxine is 100 mcg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And venlafaxine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 75 mg in the morning and 37.5 mg at night. And don’t forget—start ruxolitinib when you get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll write that down. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try to stay active with your walker, but avoid heavy lifting. Keep your wounds clean and dry, and follow up with dermatology and wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my fiancée knows what to watch for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. She’s listed as your emergency contact. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge summary is ready. You were admitted for fever, likely from your skin wounds, and we treated you with IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And everything else—heart, thyroid, mood—was addressed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your heart function is stable on metoprolol, your thyroid dose was adjusted, and your depression management was updated. Your GVHD and pain are being managed with current meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad to see you improving. The team will review your follow-up appointments before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are signed. You can go home now. Keep taking your meds, watch for fever or swelling, and call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll follow up with all my specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right track. Stay in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.text: Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.text: Let us know how you’re doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will, thanks.

conversation_lines.text: You’re all set.

conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.text: Bye.
